title: PV Sindhu Has Lost Nine Straight Matches to An Se Young. She Is Thirty and Running Out of Answers.
excerpt: The two-time Olympic medalist fell 21-17, 21-14 in the Singapore Open quarterfinals. No Indian woman reached the singles semifinals. The 2028 Olympics are two years away and the world's best player has her number completely.
body:
PV Sindhu walked off the court at the Singapore Indoor Stadium on Friday for the ninth consecutive time without beating An Se Young. The score read 21-17, 21-14. The match lasted 48 minutes. The losing streak now stretches back to the 2022 Commonwealth Games final — more than three and a half years of trying and failing against the same opponent.

Sindhu is thirty years old. She has an Olympic silver medal from Rio 2016 and a bronze from Tokyo 2020. She is a former world champion. And since 2022, she has been unable to find a way past the 24-year-old South Korean who has reshaped the upper tier of women's badminton into a one-player event.

## The Pattern That Will Not Break

The match in Singapore followed a script that Sindhu and her coaching team must know by heart. She came out aggressive, matched An Se Young point for point until 7-7 in the first game, and then watched the Korean pull away with a five-point run that broke the rhythm of the match. Sindhu clawed back to 17-19, won the longest rally of the contest, and then gifted the game away with two unforced errors.

In the second game, An raced to a 6-0 lead before Sindhu had time to settle. The Indian fought back to 12-14 after winning a punishing 30-shot rally — the kind of physical exchange that used to be her signature. But the effort left her emptied. An scored four of the next five points and sealed the match on her second match point when Sindhu sent a return long.

An Se Young has lost one match in all of 2026. One. In 32 outings. She is the reigning Olympic champion, the reigning world number one, and the most dominant force in women's badminton since Zhang Ning two decades ago.

## Nine Matches, One Game Won

Sindhu has managed to take a single game off An Se Young in their last nine meetings — at the 2023 Badminton Asia Championships. That is the only time she has extended the Korean to three games in nearly four years.

The head-to-head tells a story that goes beyond tactics. An is faster to the net. Her court coverage is more efficient. Her ability to win the crucial points — the 18-all, 19-all moments that define close games — is simply superior. Sindhu still has the power, the reach, and the experience. What she lacks is the pace of adjustment. By the time she figures out An's pattern in any given game, the Korean has already moved on to the next one.

## What This Means for India's Badminton Future

Sindhu's exit from the Singapore Open means no Indian woman reached the singles semifinals at a Super 750 event again. Malvika Bansod and Unnati Hooda fell in the opening rounds. The pipeline behind Sindhu remains thin.

The good news came from the doubles court. Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty — the reigning Asian Games champions and world number four pair — survived a scare against Malaysia's Kang Khai Xing and Aaron Tai before winning 19-21, 21-17, 21-13 to reach the semifinals. Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto also advanced in the mixed doubles after their Malaysian opponents retired due to injury.

But Indian badminton has depended on Sindhu's star power for a decade. The question now is not whether she can still compete at the highest level — she clearly can. It is whether she can compete at the very highest level, against the very best player in the world, in the matches that matter most.

## The Road Ahead

Sindhu's current world ranking is 11, down from a career-high of number two. The Women's T20 World Cup is not her concern, but the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics are. She will be 33 by then. If she is to win a third Olympic medal — which would make her the most decorated Indian Olympian in history — she will need to find a way past the player who has owned her for nearly four years.

For NRIs who have followed Sindhu since that electric run in Rio — when she became the face of Indian sport for an entire generation — the Singapore loss carries a particular weight. She is no longer the young prodigy upsetting the established order. She is the established order being upset. The question is whether the fire that took her to two Olympic podiums can survive nine consecutive reminders that the sport has moved forward without her.

The answer will have to come on the court. And the next chance is not far away.
